title: Basic Evaluate Call
background:
JsonE.Net can evaluate templates with a single call to `JsonE.Evaluate(template)`. This is the simplest integration path and keeps calling code minimal.

This lesson focuses on wiring that basic evaluation call and returning the library result unchanged.
instructions: Evaluate the provided template using the library API and return the result.

title: Evaluate With Context
background:
When templates reference symbols, pass a context object to supply those values. JsonE.Net accepts context as a `JsonNode`, so the usual integration pattern is `JsonE.Evaluate(template, context)`.

This lesson introduces context-aware evaluation by wiring the provided context into the call.
instructions: Evaluate the template using the provided context object and return the result.

title: Custom Function Registration
background:
JsonE.Net includes built-in functions for common operations. When those built-ins are not enough, you can register custom functions by adding `JsonFunction` values to the context object. The function can then be called from expressions evaluated by `JsonE.Evaluate`.

Custom functions receive arguments as `JsonNode?[]`, which gives you direct access to JSON values passed from expressions. This lesson focuses on adding a function to context before evaluation. You are exercising the `JsonFunction.Create(...)` extension point from C# code.
instructions: Add a custom `mod` function to the context, then evaluate the template.

title: Custom Function Argument Validation
background:
Custom functions receive `JsonNode?[]` parameters. In application code, you should validate argument count and types before performing numeric or string operations, so your function fails predictably.

This lesson focuses on defensive function design. You will return `null` for invalid input instead of throwing, and otherwise return a computed JSON value.
instructions: Create a `safeDiv` custom function that returns `null` for invalid input or division by zero, otherwise `x / y`.

title: EvaluationContext Access
background:
JsonE.Net also passes an `EvaluationContext` into custom functions. This lets a function inspect currently available symbols without hard-coding every value into its argument list.

In this lesson, you will use context-aware behavior through `IsDefined(...)`. The goal is to practice the library extension point, not to teach template operators.
instructions: Add a `hasSymbol(name)` custom function that returns whether a context symbol is defined using `EvaluationContext`.

title: Deterministic Time Context
background:
Some JsonE evaluations depend on current time. `EvaluationContext` includes a default `now` value internally, based on the current clock.

For deterministic behavior in tests and repeatable workflows, set a fixed `now` in the context you pass to evaluation.
